title: Home to his mother
hook: the baby refuses every nurse until his sister leads them to his own mother

segments.voice: Yesterday: Asiya's arms, and a queen who said do not kill him. Your line was a good heart in a hard house.
screen: `A GOOD HEART IN A HARD HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Back upstream, in a small house, a mother sits very still. She's set her son on the river, and the Qur'an is plain about what that costs: the heart of Musa's mother became empty. Hollowed out. So empty she nearly gave the whole secret away, and would have, the verse says, if Allah hadn't strengthened her heart. But she doesn't just sit. She turns to her daughter, Musa's sister, and gives her one word: follow him.
screen: `A HEART GONE EMPTY.` → `SHE NEARLY TELLS.` → `FOLLOW HIM.`

segments.voice: Surah al-Qasas keeps going. The sister watches from a distance, the Qur'an says, while they didn't notice her. Picture a girl at the edge of a crowd at the palace, trying to look like she's just passing by. Inside, there's a problem. The baby won't nurse. Nurse after nurse is brought in, and he turns away from every one. The Qur'an says Allah had forbidden him the foster mothers beforehand. So the sister sees her chance. She steps forward, as innocently as she can: shall I show you a household who will raise him for you and take good care of him? And so, the verse says, We returned him to his mother, so that her eye might be cooled, and she would not grieve, and so she would know that the promise of Allah is true. On day forty-three, at the river, she was promised: We will bring him back to you. Here it is, a few verses later. And yesterday's image is back too: her eye cooled, the same delight Asiya felt, now given to the woman who bore him. Notice who makes it happen. Not an army, not a miracle anyone can see. A baby who won't feed, and a sister brave enough to speak up at the right moment. The Qur'an doesn't give the sister's name, and says no more about her after this. But without her, no homecoming. Some commentators add that the mother was even paid to nurse her own son. The text itself only says he came home.
screen: `THE SISTER WATCHES FROM AFAR.` · `HE REFUSES EVERY NURSE.` · `SHALL I SHOW YOU A HOUSEHOLD?` · `THE PROMISE KEPT.` · then, large: `HER EYE COOLED.`

segments.voice: Think back for something you lost, let go of or gave up on that found its way back: a friendship that restarted after years, a thing misplaced for a month, a sense of humor after a bad season, your appetite for something you used to love. Notice who or what carried it home; often it's someone small, standing at the edge of the crowd. If you pray, give thanks for it.
Musa, the baby who refused every nurse until his sister brought him home, his mother's eye cooled at last.
Your line: what is yours returns. A heart emptied out, and a promise kept. Day forty-five, done.

screen: `DAY 45 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE BLOW AND THE FLIGHT.`

howItsDone: Muslims often point to Musa's return to his mother as a sign that Allah's promises are kept, and teachers use the story with children to talk about trust.

original.note: Arabic, from Qur'an 28:10: "empty" — the heart of Musa's mother after she let him go.

trapdoor: what you thought: a lucky coincidence.
what it means: a promise kept. the baby refuses every nurse, his sister speaks up, and he is brought home, as his mother was told he would be.
what a scholar hears: 28:13 says he was returned "so that her eye might be cooled," the same image, from the same root, as Asiya's qurratu 'ayn a few verses earlier.
recall: a guest, someone welcomed and fed
a friend of the closest, truest kind

sources.ref: Qur'an 20:40 (the sister: shall I show you one who will nurse him?)

notes: The sister is unnamed in the Qur'an; commentators give names (e.g. Maryam or Kulthum). The script says only that she is unnamed and the sources say little more.
'Some commentators add that the mother was paid to nurse her own son': reported in tafsir; flagged as commentary. Confirm or remove.
